title: Studying Isn't Practice: Turn the Board Into a Drill Partner (Part 3 of 7)
author: How to Teach With AI
summary: The third installment of a seven-part series on using AI to build student capacity makes a fundamental distinction: studying (exposure -- re-reading, re-watching, highlighting) is not the same as practice (reps at the edge of current ability with feedback that improves each next rep). Most university students spend all their time studying and almost none practicing, which explains why they graduate with credentials but without the capacities those credentials are supposed to certify. The author argues that an AI Board of Advisors (built in Parts 1 and 2) is uniquely positioned to serve as a drill partner: it can isolate a sub-skill, design ten targeted reps, and give specific feedback on every one -- something no human tutor has the patience or availability to provide at scale. The key pedagogical move is to shift from content review to structured practice on a specific, narrow capacity. The piece provides concrete implementation guidance for turning AI from a study-enhancer into a deliberate practice partner.
points: Studying (exposure) and practice (reps with feedback at the edge of current ability) are categorically different: students can study for five hours and leave with worse retention than twenty minutes of deliberate retrieval practice.

The AI Board of Advisors, built in earlier parts of the series, serves as a drill partner that can isolate a specific sub-skill, design a targeted rep sequence, and give individual feedback -- providing the conditions of deliberate practice that most students never access.
Most undergraduates graduate with a diploma certifying knowledge of a discipline but without the actual disciplinary capacities -- because they studied the discipline rather than practiced it.

The principle underlying the argument is K. Anders Ericsson's deliberate practice: reps must be at the edge of current competence, with immediate feedback, for skill to accrue; passive re-reading meets none of these conditions.

The shift the article advocates -- from AI as study aid to AI as structured practice designer -- represents a different relationship with the tool: less 'make this easier' and more 'make me better through specific challenge and feedback.'
quotes: What produces capability is focused repetition on a specific sub-skill, at the edge of current ability, with immediate corrective feedback, over time. The reason most students don't practice like this is not that they are lazy.

The sweet spot is the zone where you can do it about 60 to 80 percent of the time, and where the failures are informative.
